extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTAB/USPTO officials, litigants in inter partes review, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Statutory and procedural standards governing institution, scope, and final decisions in inter partes review (IPR) proceedings before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board and the Director of the USPTO. Focuses on petition content, institution threshold, scope of review, and available judicial review/remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition content and particularity (§311(a), §312(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to institute an inter partes review must identify each claim challenged and the grounds for challenge with particularity; the petition 'may request to cancel as unpatentable 1 or more claims of the patent' (grounds include lack of novelty or obviousness under §§102 and 103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition is the centerpiece of the proceeding: it should enumerate each claim challenged, the specific grounds for each claim, and supporting evidence. The Court emphasizes that the petition, not the Director, defines the proceeding’s contours. (See §§311(a), 312(a)(3).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary response by patent owner (§313)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner may file a preliminary response to the petition explaining why no inter partes review should be instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations must permit a response to the petition; the response is directed at the petition’s contents (not at a later-instituted subset of claims). Use the preliminary response to challenge sufficiency/particularity of petitioned grounds and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s institution threshold (§314(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before instituting IPR, the Director must determine 'there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a threshold screening standard: a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one challenged claim justifies institution. The Court reads this as consistent with allowing institution based on prospect of success on a single claim, not necessarily requiring assessment of every claim at the screening stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s binary 'whether to institute' decision (§314(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director must decide 'whether to institute an inter partes review . . . pursuant to [the] petition'—a yes-or-no choice regarding instituting review 'pursuant to' (i.e., in accordance with) the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treats this language as indicating a binary choice (institute or not) and as reinforcing that the petition should define the proceeding. The Director's discretion is to institute or deny, not to create a different proceeding of his own design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of final written decision (§318(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an inter partes review is instituted and not dismissed, the Board 'shall issue a final written decision with respect to the patentability of any patent claim challenged by the petitioner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court reads 'shall' as mandatory and 'any' as expansive (i.e., 'any' in this context means every claim challenged by the petitioner), concluding the Board must address the patentability of all claims the petitioner challenged when IPR is instituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory basis for 'partial institution' power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office's asserted power of 'partial institution' (per 37 C.F.R. §42.108(a) authorizing review 'on all or some of the challenged claims') is not found in the statutory text and cannot be inferred when §318(a) requires the Board to decide 'any patent claim challenged by the petitioner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency regulations claiming a power to institute review on only some challenged claims conflict with the Court's textual reading; policy or efficiency arguments for partial institution should be directed to Congress, not invoked to override clear statutory commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner, not Director, defines proceeding contours
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress structured IPR so that the petitioner defines the proceeding’s contours: the petition identifies the claims and grounds; various provisions (e.g., §312(a)(3), §316(a)(8)) treat the petition as central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, filings, preliminary responses, and further proceedings should be aligned to the petitioned claims and grounds; departures from the petition’s scope are disfavored absent statutory text authorizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte reexamination contrast (§303(a), §304)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ex parte reexamination statute explicitly authorizes the Director to act 'on his own initiative, and at any time' and permits claim-by-claim institution limited to the 'substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim' (§303(a), §304).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress knew how to vest claim-by-claim authority in the Director; its failure to do so in the IPR provisions counsels against inferring a similar power for IPR institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner’s claims may be winnowed during proceeding (§316(d)(1)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may concede or 'cancel any challenged patent claim' during IPR, and claims challenged 'in the petition' may drop out before the end of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court explains differences in statutory phrasing (e.g., 'in the petition' vs 'challenged by the petitioner') are explained by this statutory winnowing—only claims still challenged 'by the petitioner' at the litigation’s end need be addressed in the final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural features of instituted IPR (§316, §§317)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once instituted, an IPR proceeds with discovery, briefing, an oral hearing, possible amendment of claims, and potential settlement; the patent owner may seek to amend or cancel claims (§316(d)); parties may settle (§317).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should prepare for full adversarial procedures akin to litigation once IPR is instituted, including evidence and hearing preparation for each claim the petitioner challenges and the Board will decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on judicial review (§314(d) and Cuozzo) and APA remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 314(d) states that the Director’s determination whether to institute 'shall be final and nonappealable'; Cuozzo held §314(d) precludes review of the Director’s initial determination under §314(a) (reasonable likelihood), but it does not permit agency action 'outside its statutory limits'—judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act remains available for actions 'not in accordance with law' or 'in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitations' (5 U.S.C. §§706(2)(A),(C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges that merely question the adequacy of the petition are typically precluded from review, but claims that the agency exceeded statutory bounds (e.g., instituting partial institution contrary to §318(a)) remain reviewable under APA standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference threshold for agency interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s interpretation (including a claimed power) is not owed deference under Chevron unless the statute is ambiguous after employing 'traditional tools of statutory construction'; if the statute is clear, there is no Chevron deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating agency rules or interpretations (e.g., partial institution regulation), first apply textual and contextual statutory interpretation; only if ambiguity remains consider deference and reasonableness of the agency’s interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong presumption in favor of judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'strong presumption' favoring judicial review of agency action; clear and convincing indications are required to displace reviewability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should presume reviewability unless Congress's intent to preclude review is unmistakably clear; use this presumption when assessing §314(d)'s nonappealability scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency rulemaking authority may fill gaps but cannot override clear statutory text (§316(a)(2),(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress authorized the agency to issue regulations 'setting forth the standards for the showing of sufficient grounds to institute a review' and 'establishing and governing inter partes review' (§316(a)(2),(4)), but regulations cannot create powers not supported by the statute’s text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory gap-filling is appropriate where the statute is ambiguous and Congress granted rulemaking, but agency rules that conflict with clear statutory mandates (e.g., a regulation authorizing partial institution when §318(a) is read to require decisions on all challenged claims) are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/efficiency arguments do not override statutory commands
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency arguments (e.g., that partial institution allows the Board to focus on the most promising challenges and conserve resources) are policy matters for Congress, not a basis for judicially permitting agency actions that exceed statutory wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If policy improvements are desired (like partial institution for efficiency), Congress must amend the statute; courts will enforce the statute as written rather than adopt agency-favored expedients inconsistent with statutory text.
